title: Northwest Orient Airlines 324
summary: Northwest Orient Airlines Flight 324, a Douglas C-54E military charter aircraft, crashed into Hecate Strait in British Columbia while making an emergency landing at Sandspit Airport on January 19, 1952. Engine No. 1 failed near Sitka, and the crew declared an emergency and proceeded to Sandspit on three engines. During the landing approach, the aircraft touched down about one-third down the runway, then power was reapplied at midpoint to attempt a go-around. The aircraft became airborne but settled into Hecate Strait off the end of the runway. Seven survivors were rescued from the freezing waters, while the remaining 36 perished from drowning or exposure to cold temperatures.
probable_cause: Engine No. 1 suffered an oil loss necessitating engine shutdown. Following the engine failure, the crew elected to land at the nearest suitable airport rather than continue to destination on three engines, consistent with company procedures. The aborted landing and go-around attempt resulted in the aircraft settling into the water during climbout.

factors.evidence: pilots reported a failure of engine No. 1 with rapid loss of oil pressure
after a short time on the ground, engine power was re-applied and the plane took off again

events.text: Aircraft departed Elmendorf Air Force Base in Anchorage at 21:11 on three-engine flight to McChord Air Force Base.
Pilots reported failure of engine No. 1 near Sitka with rapid loss of oil pressure in that engine.
Pilots requested weather forecasts at nearby airports in Annette, Sandspit, and Port Hardy and decided to make an emergency landing at Sandspit.
Aircraft touched down about one-third down the runway at Sandspit and after a short time on the ground, engine power was reapplied and the plane took off again.
Aircraft settled into Hecate Strait off the end of the runway and seven survivors were rescued from the freezing waters shortly after the crash.

title: American Airlines 6780
summary: On 22 January 1952, American Airlines Flight 6780, a Convair 240, was on final approach to Newark Airport using the instrument landing system when it crashed into a house in Elizabeth, New Jersey, approximately 3.4 miles southwest of Newark. The aircraft had gone 2,100 feet off course to the right. All 23 occupants on board plus 7 people on the ground were killed. The cause of the crash was never determined.

crashed at 3:45 p.m. into a house at the intersection of Williamson and South Streets, in the city of Elizabeth, New Jersey

title: 1952 Air France SNCASE Languedoc crash
summary: The aircraft crashed shortly after takeoff from Nice Airport when the co-pilot's aileron controls jammed due to a chain slipping off its sprocket. The aircraft banked to the left, rolled onto its back and crashed about 1 km north of the airport, killing all 38 people on board. A design fault in the difficulty of setting and inspecting the chains in dual control columns contributed to the accident.
probable_cause: Aileron control jamming due to chain slipping off sprocket in dual control system.

factors.evidence: The difficulty of setting and inspecting the chains in the dual control columns was cited as a contributory factor in the accident.
The chain had slipped off its sprocket and was not detected during inspection.
The co-pilot's aileron controls had jammed due to a chain slipping off its sprocket.
The aircraft was seen to bank to the left, roll onto its back and crash about 1 km north of the airport.

events.text: Shortly after take-off from Nice Airport on a scheduled domestic passenger flight to Le Bourget Airport, Paris, the aircraft was seen to bank to the left, roll onto its back and crash about 1 km north of the airport.
The co-pilot's aileron controls had jammed due to a chain slipping off its sprocket.
The accident was the third deadliest in France at the time and is the deadliest involving the SNCASE Languedoc.

title: KLM 592
summary: The Douglas DC-6 departed Rome-Ciampino for Frankfurt Airport on 22 March 1952. At approximately 10:45 AM, the crew reported descending to 2,460 feet near the Offenbach beacon. Nothing more was heard from the flight, and the aircraft crashed into a forest approximately five minutes later. Of 47 occupants, 45 perished. The cause could not be determined, but investigation suggested the crew may have continued the approach below the minimum descent altitude to maintain visual contact with the ground.
probable_cause: The cause of the crash was not determined. It is possible that the crew continued the approach below the minimum descent altitude to maintain a visual contact with the ground, resulting in controlled flight into terrain.

notes: Cause not determined; only speculation about descent below minimums; limited investigation details available

title: Japan Air Lines 301
summary: Flight 301 took off from Tokyo-Haneda Airport on 9 April 1952 on scheduled flight to Fukuoka. While flight 301 was cruising approximately 62 miles south of Tokyo in marginal weather conditions, the aircraft crashed into the slope of Mount Mihara on Izu Ōshima. All 37 people on board were killed. The aircraft had deviated from its original course.
probable_cause: Navigational error by pilots resulting in deviation from original course. Exact cause could not be determined due to lack of cockpit voice recorder or flight data recorder, and occupation authorities refused to provide ATC tape recording.

factors.evidence: aircraft was cruising in marginal weather conditions
aircraft had deviated from its original course

title: Pan Am 526A
summary: Pan Am Flight 526A ditched in the Atlantic Ocean after both engines lost power shortly after takeoff from San Juan. Engine number 3 failed at 350 feet and engine number 4 failed at 550 feet. The investigation revealed inadequate maintenance: engine 3 had not been changed when metal shavings were found in the engine oil, leading to its failure immediately after takeoff. The crew performed a water landing, but survivors panicked and refused to board life rafts, resulting in 52 deaths.
probable_cause: Engine number 3 was not changed when metal shavings were found in the engine oil in maintenance before this flight, leading to its failure immediately subsequent to take-off. The pilots' attempt to re-establish a climb without using all available power after the loss of power from the second engine led to a nose high pitch attitude and rapid decrease of airspeed.

title: Pan Am 202
summary: A Boeing 377 Stratocruiser registered N1039V, christened Clipper Good Hope, was operating an international scheduled passenger flight from Rio de Janeiro to Port of Spain, the third leg of a four-leg journey from Buenos Aires. The aircraft departed Rio at 2:43 a.m. on April 29, 1952 and was last heard from at 6:16 a.m. reporting abeam the city of Barreiras in eastern Brazil at 14,500 feet. It was expected to report abeam Carolina at 7:45 a.m. but the aircraft never reported again. Investigation of the wreckage found evidence indicating the No. 2 engine and propeller had failed in flight, causing the aircraft to break apart. It crashed in the dense Amazon jungle approximately 281 nautical miles southwest of Carolina. All 50 people aboard were killed.
probable_cause: The exact cause of the crash was not established. However, investigation of wreckage indicated that an engine had likely separated in flight after propeller blade failure, with the propeller failure causing the engine to experience highly unbalanced loads that eventually caused separation from the aircraft.

factors.evidence: evidence on the port wing root, the No. 2 engine nacelle, the leading edge of the vertical stabilizer, and the horizontal stabilizer led investigators to believe that the engine and/or propeller had failed in flight
the engine separation would have precipitated loss of control
the propeller failure caused the engine to experience highly unbalanced loads and it eventually separated from the aircraft, precipitating an in-flight breakup
a huge fire had consumed the fuselage

events.text: Flight 202 departed Rio de Janeiro at 2:43 a.m. on April 29, 1952 on an off-airways route directly to Port of Spain over the Amazon jungle
At 6:16 a.m. local time the flight reported abeam the city of Barreiras in eastern Brazil, flying at 14,500 feet under VFR conditions
The aircraft failed to report abeam Carolina at the estimated time of 7:45 a.m. as expected, and then failed to report abeam the city of Santarém in northern Brazil
Local authorities initiated a missing aircraft alert when all subsequent position reports failed to arrive

A properly equipped investigation team finally reached the wreckage on August 15, finding it had fallen to the ground in three main sections across dense forest 13 nautical miles northwest of their base camp, confirming all on board had died on impact and a huge fire had consumed the fuselage

notes: Exact cause not established due to difficult terrain and investigation conditions; propeller failure and engine separation is theorized based on wreckage examination

title: 1952 Mount Gannett C-124 crash
summary: A Douglas C-124 Globemaster II departed Washington for Alaska on November 22, 1952. Severe weather with heavy clouds, dense fog, and swirling snow obscured visibility, forcing the aircraft to fly without visual references using only altitude, a radio beacon, and a stopwatch. The aircraft crashed into Mount Gannett at approximately 8,100 ft during descent to Elmendorf Air Force Base.

events.text: Weather near Elmendorf at the time was severe with heavy clouds, dense fog, and swirling snow which obscured visibility.
Around 4pm, a distress call was received by the pilot of a Northwest Orient Airlines passenger aircraft.
The wreckage of the aircraft was found on November 28, 1952, on the south side of Mount Gannett by Terris Moore from the Fairbanks Civil Air Patrol and Lieutenant Thomas Sullivan.

title: 1952 Bermuda air crash
summary: Douglas DC-4 registered CU-T397 arrived at Kindley field at 3:30 am on 6 December 1952. After refuelling, it departed at 4:45 am with 34 passengers and crew of eight. About a minute after taking off, an explosion occurred, and the plane crashed into the sea. The accident killed 37 of the 42 occupants.
probable_cause: Cause of accident never determined. Explosion occurred approximately one minute after takeoff. Possibly while still pushing engines hard to gain altitude.

title: 1952 Moses Lake C-124 crash
summary: A United States Air Force Douglas C-124 Globemaster II transport aircraft carrying 105 passengers and 10 crew departed Larson Air Force Base near Moses Lake, Washington on December 20, 1952 as part of Operation Sleigh Ride to bring servicemen home from Korea. Just seconds after taking off, the left wing struck the ground and the aircraft cartwheeled, broke up and exploded. Investigation revealed the elevator and rudder gust locks had not been disengaged prior to departure.
probable_cause: The aircraft's elevator and rudder gust locks had not been disengaged prior to departure, causing loss of control during takeoff.
